Cloud Computing Fundamentals
What is Cloud Computing?
Cloud Computing is the delivery of computing resources such as servers, storage, databases, networking, 
software, and processing power over the Internet.
Instead of purchasing and maintaining physical hardware, users can access computing resources whenever 
required and usually pay based on usage.
Example: Google Drive allows users to store files on cloud servers instead of storing everything on their 
computer.

Characteristics of Cloud Computing 
1. On-Demand Self-Service
Users can access computing resources such as servers, storage, and applications whenever they need them, 
without human interaction with the service provider.
Example: Creating a virtual machine instantly on a cloud platform. 
2. Broad Network Access
Cloud services are available through the Internet using devices such as:
● Computers
● Smartphones
● Tablets
● IoT devices
3. Resource Pooling
The cloud provider uses a shared pool of computing resources to serve multiple users.
Resources include:
● CPU
● Memory
● Storage
● Network bandwidth

Cloud resources can be quickly increased or decreased according to demand.

● Storage used
● CPU usage
● Network traffic
● Number of requests

Cloud Deployment Models
What is a Cloud Deployment Model?
A cloud deployment model defines where your cloud infrastructure lives, who owns and manages it, and how it is
accessed. It establishes the boundaries of your cloud environment, dictating what you can customize, how
resources are shared among users, and the overarching purpose of the setup.
Understanding these models is the crucial first step for any business migrating to the cloud, as each offers distinct
trade-offs in governance, cost, security, and management.
A cloud deployment model describes where the cloud infrastructure is located, who owns it, and who can 
access it.
There are three commonly discussed deployment models:
1. Public Cloud
2. Private Cloud
3. Hybrid Cloud

control over cloud resources.

How to Choose the Right Deployment Model
There is no one-size-fits-all approach. The ideal choice depends entirely on your specific business
requirements. Consider these five factors:
● Cost: Determine your budget for upfront capital expenses versus ongoing operational expenses.
● Scalability: Assess your current traffic and predict how rapidly you will need to scale resources in
the future.
● Ease of Use: Evaluate the technical expertise of your internal IT staff and their ability to manage
complex infrastructures.
● Compliance: Identify any legal or industry regulations (like HIPAA or GDPR) that dictate where
and how your data must be stored.
● Privacy: Classify your data to determine what can be public and what requires strict, isolated
confidentiality.

Virtualization 
Virtualization is the process of creating a virtual version of computing resources such as servers, 
storage, networks, or operating systems using software.
In cloud computing, virtualization allows one physical server to run multiple virtual machines 
(VMs). Each VM behaves like an independent computer.

slides.text:
Hypervisor types
Type 1: Bare-Metal Hypervisors
Type 1 hypervisors run directly on the physical hardware of the host computer, completely bypassing a host operating 
system.
● High Efficiency: They have direct access to physical hardware, which eliminates performance overhead.
● Strong Security: The compromise of one virtual machine does not affect the others because there is no 
underlying host OS to exploit.
● Enterprise Focus: They are the standard choice for data centers, server farms, and corporate cloud environments.
● Common Examples: VMware ESXi, Microsoft Hyper-V, and KVM (Kernel-based Virtual Machine).
Type 2: Hosted Hypervisors
Type 2 hypervisors install and run as a standard software application on top of an existing host operating system. 
● Simple Setup: They are easy to install, configure, and use without modifying server hardware.
● Performance Overhead: They must pass all resource requests through the host OS, making them slower than 
Type 1.
● Consumer Focus: They are primarily used by developers, testers, and regular users to run legacy apps or test 
software locally.
● Common Examples: Oracle VirtualBox, VMware Workstation, and Parallels Desktop.

Types of virtualization
1. Server Virtualization
● Splits one physical server into many independent virtual machines (VMs).
● Each VM runs its own operating system.
● Maximizes hardware use and lowers physical server counts. 
2. Desktop Virtualization
● Runs user desktop environments on a remote central server rather than a local hard drive.
● Lets users securely access their personalized desktop from any device.
● Commonly known as Virtual Desktop Infrastructure (VDI)
3. Network Virtualization
● Combines physical and software-based network resources into a single virtual unit.
● Separates network functions like routing and firewalls from physical hardware.
● Forms programmable networks often managed through IBM software-defined networking 
(SDN) tools.

4. Storage Virtualization
● Pools physical storage from multiple network devices into a single virtual storage space.
● Managed centrally to ease data backup, archiving, and recovery.
● Simplifies capacity expansion across mixed hardware brands. 
5. Application Virtualization
● Runs software programs separate from the underlying host operating system.
● Keeps applications in isolated bubbles to prevent system conflicts.
● Allows programs to run without a traditional installation on the local device. 
6. Operating System (OS) Virtualization / Containers
● Shares a single OS kernel across multiple isolated user spaces (containers).
● Lighter and faster than full hardware virtual machines.
● Packs software tightly for rapid application deployment.

Resource Management
Resource management is the process of efficiently allocating and controlling cloud resources such as CPU, 
memory, storage, bandwidth, and virtual machines.
IoT systems may have thousands or millions of connected devices, so resources need to be managed efficiently.
Major activities
1. Resource allocation – Assigning resources to IoT applications.
2. Resource monitoring – Checking CPU, memory, storage, and network usage.
3. Load balancing – Distributing workload among multiple servers.
4. Resource scheduling – Deciding when and where tasks should execute.
5. Resource optimization – Avoiding unnecessary resource consumption.

Scalability and Elasticity 
Cloud Elasticity
Cloud elasticity refers to the ability of a cloud environment to dynamically and
automatically expand or compress infrastructural resources based on sudden fluctuations in
demand.

automatically expand or compress infrastructural resources based on sudden fluctuations in

slides.text:
Key Characteristics:
● Dynamic Adjustment: Automatically provisions extra compute, storage, or network resources
(CPU, Memory, Bandwidth) when client access expands, and reduces them when traffic drops.
● Cost Efficiency: Maximizes resource utilization and minimizes infrastructure costs. It is most
commonly associated with public cloud pay-per-use models where you only pay for the duration
resources are consumed.
● Horizontal Scaling: Typically relies on scale-out arrangements (adding or removing instances
dynamically) rather than upgrading existing hardware.
● Best For: Unpredictable workloads or scenarios where resource requirements fluctuate up and
down suddenly for specific time intervals. It is not practical for environments requiring a
persistent infrastructure for a constant heavy workload.
● Mission-Critical Performance: Ensures that applications maintain performance requirements
during sudden spikes, preventing potential business losses due to downtime or latency.
Example: Consider an online shopping site. During the Christmas festive season, the transaction
workload suddenly spikes. For this specific period, resources need to scale up to handle the traffic. Once
the holiday season ends, the deployed resources are automatically withdrawn. Cloud elasticity perfectly
addresses this temporary, dynamic need.

sudden, temporary spikes.
● Capacity Planning: Focuses on upgrading or adding resources to work efficiently with
growing software or applications.
● Pay-Per-Use: Like elasticity, scalability is often billed on a pay-per-use basis, but the

permanent workload, you request your cloud vendor to scale up your database capacity.

to potential downtime.
2. Downtime for Upgrades: Sometimes you need to stop everything to make upgrades which can disrupt
services.
3. It may not be able to handle sudden spikes in traffic as if the servers capacity is reached, additional
resources may not be available.

Implementation Methods of Scaling in Cloud Computing
The following are the implementation methods of Scaling in Cloud Computing:
1. Auto Scaling
Cloud platforms such as AWS (Amazon web services), Microsoft Azure and Google cloud platform provide auto scaling
capabilities. It allows users to automatically adjust resources based on predefined conditions such as CPU utilization,
network traffic or application load.
2. Serverless Computing
With serverless computing, cloud providers manage the underlying infrastructure and users only pay for the resources
consumed by their applications. Serverless platforms automatically scale resources based on the incoming requests and
allow applications to handle varying workloads without manual intervention.
3. Elastic Load Balancing
Load balancers distribute the incoming traffic across the multiple instances to ensure that no single instance becomes
overwhelmed. This helps in achieving horizontal scalability by adding or removing instances based on the patterns of
traffic.
4. Containers and Container Orchestration
Different technologies like Docker and Kubernetes enable organizations to build and manage containerized applications
that can scale horizontally across clusters of servers. Container orchestration platforms automatically scale containers
based on demand.

Cloud elasticity refers to the ability of a cloud environment to dynamically and automatically expand or
compress infrastructural resources based on sudden fluctuations in demand.
Example: Consider an online shopping site. During the Christmas festive season, the transaction
workload suddenly spikes. For this specific period, resources need to scale up to handle the traffic. Once
the holiday season ends, the deployed resources are automatically withdrawn. Cloud elasticity perfectly
addresses this temporary, dynamic need.

during sudden spikes, preventing potential business losses due to downtime or latency.

Benefits of cloud elasticity
● Cost savings – With cloud elasticity, you pay only for the resources you use. You also save on costs by 
using cloud resources and don’t have to purchase or manage equipment on-premises. Elasticity 
eliminates over-provisioning, which can cut into budgets.
● Increased flexibility – You can quickly adapt to evolving market trends or pivot when business spikes. 
No worries about under-provisioning and being caught unprepared when demand skyrockets.
● Enhanced availability and resiliency – Elastic cloud resources means you always have compute, 
storage, and memory when you need it. And because it’s so easy and quick to spin up new resources, 
you increase resiliency and avoid downtime with automatic replication when virtual machines fail.
● Competitive edge – With the ability to stay flexible, adapt on the fly to customer and market demands, 
and speed time to market, you can gain a competitive advantage.

Device-to-cloud communication core architecture links physical edge nodes to centralized cloud 
platforms. It uses lightweight protocols like MQTT, secure gateways, and streaming brokers to 
process telemetry data and push commands reliably across distributed networks. 
Core Layers
● Device Layer: Comprises microcontrollers, sensors, and actuators that gather raw physical 
data from the local environment. [
● Gateway/Edge Layer: Acts as a local bridge or pre-processor. It filters data, aggregates 
local packets, and translates short-range protocols (like Bluetooth or Zigbee) to wide-area 
network formats. 
● Communication Layer: Uses lightweight transport protocols such as MQTT, 
HTTP/HTTPS, or CoAP over Wi-Fi, cellular, or LoRaWAN networks. 
● Cloud Ingestion Layer: Uses scalable message brokers like Apache Kafka or cloud-native 
endpoints to securely receive, authenticate, and buffer incoming device streams. 
● Processing & Application Layer: Stores raw data in data lakes, processes real-time 
analytics, and exposes dashboards or user control apps.

App-to-Cloud Communication in Medical IoT
Once a mobile app receives data from a medical device, it must communicate with the cloud to send data and receive commands or updates. The 
communication method affects performance, latency, security, and reliability. Three common approaches are Web APIs, MQTT-based messaging, and 
Push Notifications. Each method is suitable for different medical IoT requirements.
1. Web APIs
● Uses HTTPS to exchange data between app and cloud.
● Simple, flexible, and widely supported.
● Commonly uses JSON for data exchange.
● Supports authentication and authorization.
2. IoT Services (MQTT)
● Suitable for near real-time communication.
● Works well with intermittent connectivity.
● Messages can be queued and delivered later.
● Provides reliable communication using MQTT + TLS.
3. Push Notifications
● Notify users/apps about commands, settings, or updates.
● Useful when the app is not currently active.
● Notifications may be delayed or lost.
● Should not be the only method for critical data.
4. Security
● Use HTTPS/TLS to encrypt data.
● Authentication verifies the communicating party.
● Authorization controls access and actions.
● Certificates, PKI, and mTLS can provide stronger security.

Engineering for Real-World Reliability
Reliable communication is important in connected medical devices because data loss can affect patient records and 
clinical decisions.
 Medical IoT systems must handle poor connectivity, device limitations, and cloud failures.
 Techniques such as message queuing, acknowledgments, retries, and offline storage improve reliability.
MQTT Reliability
● Local queuing: Store data on the device when offline.
● Acknowledgment: Remove data only after successful delivery.
● Retry mechanism: Resend failed messages when the connection returns.
● At-least-once delivery: Messages are retried until received.
Web API Reliability
● Retry with exponential backoff: Retry failed requests gradually.
● Timeouts: Prevent the application from waiting indefinitely.
● Circuit breaker: Temporarily stop requests after repeated failures.
● Offline queuing: Store data and send it when connectivity returns.
● Idempotency: Prevent duplicate data when requests are retried.

slides.text: System Architecture

3. Working
Step 1 – Data Collection:
 Sensors continuously measure soil moisture, temperature and humidity.
Step 2 – IoT Gateway:
 An ESP32/Raspberry Pi acts as the gateway. It collects sensor readings, filters unnecessary data and performs basic 
local processing.
Step 3 – Communication:
 The gateway sends the processed data to the cloud using MQTT or HTTPS.
Step 4 – Data Ingestion:
 A service such as AWS IoT Core or Azure IoT Hub receives the incoming sensor data and makes it available for 
further processing.
Step 5 – Cloud Processing:
 The data is stored and analyzed to identify conditions such as low soil moisture.
Step 6 – Visualization:
 The farmer can view real-time sensor readings through a web or mobile dashboard.
Step 7 – Automated Action:
 If soil moisture falls below a predefined threshold, the system can activate the irrigation pump.
